text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter says.

1. **Who is it addressed to, and who signs it?** Do you have the name of the admissions office or person, and the exact program title? I also need your name, the farm's name, your title, and the phone or email you want them to use. Does the college ask recommenders to answer specific questions, or is it an open letter?

2. **The five weeks away last summer.** I'd mention it briefly. A family emergency handled honestly reads well, and covering it ourselves is better than leaving a gap someone asks about later. Some details would help. Did he arrange cover for his shift, or help you find it? Did you hold his job for him? Did he come back when he said he would? If you'd rather leave it out, tell me.

3. **Written English.** The committee will probably notice this in his application, so the letter should deal with it directly. What do you see him do in writing at work? Does he enter notes or health records in the herd software? Do you know what level the night class is, or have you noticed him getting better?

4. **The 9 mastitis cases.** Do you know what catching them early saved? For example, cows kept in the herd, milk you didn't have to dump, lower vet or treatment costs, or a rough dollar figure. A concrete result makes this the strongest part of the letter.

5. **Signs he's ready to study.** Has he done anything beyond his assigned work, like training other workers, asking why you do things a certain way, or suggesting a change you adopted? The committee is judging whether he'll do well in a classroom, not just on the farm.

6. **His future with you.** Would you hire him back after the program, or would you have him work part-time while he's enrolled? A farm manager saying "I want him back with these skills" counts for a lot. Only say yes if you mean it.

Also: is there anything else the college might find out on its own that we should get ahead of?

1. I don't have a contact name or the exact program title, it's just "agricultural technology." It goes in through the college's online portal, due Feb 1. I don't know if they ask specific questions. I'm Mike Hollis, farm manager at Hollis Dairy. Phone is 555-0187, and I'm fine taking a call from the committee. His full name is Tomás Reyes.

2. Yes, mention it. He got his cousin, who'd worked for us before, to cover his shifts. He came back the day he said he would.

3. I don't know what he writes in the software or what level the class is. One thing: he failed the written test in a dairy safety course once and passed it the second time.

4. The vet said catching them early saved us about $8,000.

5. Don't know of anything beyond what I told you.

6. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program. I can't pay any of his tuition.

Nothing else I can think of.

I left the date line off because the portal will timestamp it. Add one if you upload it as a PDF.

<final_document>
Dear Admissions Committee,

I am writing to recommend Tomás Reyes for the two-year agricultural technology program. I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow operation, and I have supervised Tomás for the three years he has worked here, since he was 19.

Tomás runs our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, five days a week. Nobody else is there at that hour, so the shift depends on him showing up and doing the work right. In three years he has missed two shifts.

He also learned our herd management software, and he now uses it to flag sick cows for our vet. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early. Our vet estimates that saved the farm about $8,000. He learned this on the job, without formal training. Your program teaches the knowledge behind that work, and I believe he will put it to use.

There are two other things you should know. Last summer his father fell seriously ill in Mexico, and Tomás was away for five weeks. He gave me two days' notice. Before he left, he arranged for his cousin, who had worked for us before, to cover his shifts, and he came back on the day he said he would. He took care of his family without leaving us short, and I count that in his favor.

His spoken English is good. His written English is weaker, and he knows it. He is taking a night class to improve it. He once failed the written test in a dairy safety course, then passed it on his second try. He did not let that stop him, and I don't expect written work in your program to stop him either.

I will keep his job open for him part-time on weekends while he is enrolled.

I would be glad to speak with the committee. Please call me at 555-0187.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
</final_document>

Some notes before you send it:

- **The safety test:** I put it in because a second-try pass next to the night class shows him sticking with something hard. The letter still works without it. If the college already has his course records, it's better that they hear about it from you. Otherwise, cutting it is your call.
- **What I left out:** Tuition doesn't matter for admission, so the letter doesn't mention it.
- **Check the portal:** Before Feb 1, see whether the portal asks recommenders specific questions or gives a word limit. If it does, send them to me and I'll adjust the letter to fit.
